title: 'I was given electric shocks to knock the homosexuality out of my brain'

input.lead: People who were subjected to electric shocks to change their sexuality demand the government apologises
input.summary: People who were subjected to electric shocks to change their sexuality demand the government apologises
input.evidence_text: 'I was given electric shocks to knock the homosexuality out of my brain' - BBC News Image caption, Norman Goodman underwent controversial electric shock therapy By Hayley Hassall BBC North West Investigations Published 1 hour ago More victims of controversial electric shock therapy used to try to change their sexuality have come forward to call on the government to investigate the historical "scandal". They spoke out after the BBC revealed that more than 260 people had been subjected to the discredited treatment at NHS hospitals in the 1960s and 1970s. The people, who are now in their 70s and 80s, said they had been left physically and emotionally traumatised by their experiences. And while the government said it would be drafting legislation to ban "aversion therapy", ten months on, the people spoken to by the BBC said they were still yet to receive an apology for what they had endured. The BBC's investigation uncovered evidence that LGBT+ patients were subjected to electric shock aversion therapy in NHS hospitals across England. Patients were shown images associated with same-sex attraction while being given painful electric shocks in an attempt to change their sexuality. Image caption, Norman came forward following an earlier BBC investigation into electric shock therapy Norman Goodman, 75, said that from childhood he felt more like a girl than a boy, and told his parents that he wanted to be female. He was admitted to a psychiatric hospital in Manchester when he was 18, in the late 1960s. He told the BBC doctors said they would try to make it easier for him, but he was given electric shocks. title: Lindow Moss peatland housing approved with 'heavy hearts'

input.lead: One councillor says the authority "did not have a chance in hell" of winning an appeal if refused
input.summary: One councillor says the authority "did not have a chance in hell" of winning an appeal if refused
input.evidence_text: Lindow Moss peatland housing approved with 'heavy hearts' - BBC News Image caption, Members of the public and local councillors attended the meeting at Macclesfield Town Hall By Kaleigh Watterson Cheshire political reporter , Reporting from Macclesfield, Cheshire Published 1 hour ago Plans to build 125 houses on peatland in Cheshire have been approved by councillors, who said they backed the plans "with a heavy heart". The site off Cumber Lane in Wilmslow is close to where the Lindow Man - a 2,000 year old bog body - was found in the 1980s. One councillor said he voted for the plans because the council did not "have a chance in hell of actually winning an appeal". Councillor Mark Goldsmith, who spoke against the plans, said councillors "get blamed but this is national policy in practice" while a local resident said the decision was "hugely, hugely disappointing". The government has been approached for comment. Hundreds of objections had been submitted and members of the public attended the meeting of Cheshire East's strategic planning board. David Wilson, from Protect Lindow Moss, said there were "extensive reasons" to refuse the plans. "Today you are making a decision to prevent permanent and irreversible harm to land of recognised historic and environmental importance," he said. Image caption, The site was removed from the green belt under Cheshire East Council's 2017 local plan Independent David Jefferay read a statement on behalf of the local MP, Conservative Esther McVey. She said she wanted to comment because of "immense concern for the precedent this application would set in terms of large-scale development on peatland". title: Work to restore Manchester's Chinatown archway underway

input.lead: The gateway into Manchester's Chinatown is in need of significant repairs, the city council says
input.summary: The gateway into Manchester's Chinatown is in need of significant repairs, the city council says
input.evidence_text: Work to restore Manchester's Chinatown archway underway - BBC News Image source, Manchester City Council Image caption, The Grade II-listed landmark was a gift from Beijing to the people of Manchester Published 1 hour ago Work has started on the restoration of a landmark archway in Manchester's Chinatown. The Grade II-listed feature was a gift from Beijing to the people of the city in the mid 1980s. The gateway into the city's Chinatown is now in need of significant repairs which is estimated to take two years to complete, Manchester City Council said. Councillor Mandie Shilton Godwin said while the arch will be missed during the work "rest assured it will be worth the wait". Image caption, The work on the archway was a "priority", said councillor Mandie Shilton Godwin The work is part of a wider regeneration of the Chinatown area. Improvements have already been carried out earlier this year to make repairs to the large pagoda, new bespoke benches have been installed, and works are planned within the month to make repairs to the smaller pagoda. Shilton Godwin, executive member for clean air, environment and transport, said the arch has been a focal point for the Chinese community in Manchester for generations and ensuring it remains standing proudly for years to come was a "priority". "We know the significance this area holds for many of our residents and that's why we are committing to further investment, ensuring that it's not only a top destination for tourists visiting Manchester, but a community that local people feel proud to live and work in." She added: "During this two-year project we know that the arch will be missed, but rest assured it will be worth the wait." title: Manchester 'historic gem' library in line for £6.4m revamp

input.lead: The Grade II* listed Portico Library in Manchester city centre dates back to 1806
input.summary: The Grade II* listed Portico Library in Manchester city centre dates back to 1806
input.evidence_text: Manchester 'historic gem' library in line for £6.4m revamp - BBC News Image source, Andrew Brooks Image caption, The Portico Library was built in 1806 By Richard Stead North West , Reporting from in Manchester Published 1 hour ago A Manchester library described as an "architectural gem" has been awarded a restoration grant of £6.4m which will see it open up all three floors for the first time in a century. The Grade II* listed Portico Library in the city centre dates back to 1806. The cash from the National Lottery Heritage Fund will help with urgent repairs, create new spaces and a bookshop featuring Northern writers and publishers as well as a kitchen where people can explore Manchester's food culture. Dr Thom Keep, the library's chief executive and librarian, said it was a "landmark moment" in Portico's history and the changes would give people greater access to its 25,000 books and archive material. Image caption, Dr Thom Keep said the award was a "landmark moment" in the library's complex history Keep told BBC Radio Manchester the money was a major milestone in the £12m Portico Reunited campaign to "reunite this extraordinary building and make room for people to discover, learn and create together". The architectural plans will provide people step free access to the building making it easier for people to enter and move around the library. Currently, the stairs limit access and the library only occupies the first floor. Keep believes there will be a huge rise in visitors, which currently top about 30,000 a year. He said: "We're expecting that once we reopen 95,000 people will come and visit the space per year." title: Prestwich road closed by third sinkhole in 10 years

input.lead: The closure of Heywood Road follows the appearance of a third sinkhole on the same road since 2016
input.summary: The closure of Heywood Road follows the appearance of a third sinkhole on the same road since 2016
input.evidence_text: Prestwich road closed by third sinkhole in 10 years - BBC News Image caption, The sinkhole has been cordoned off and there are diversions in place By Richard Stead Reporting from in Prestwich Published 16 September 2026 Once again, a sinkhole has appeared on a road in a town in Greater Manchester - marking the third time the same road has been impacted over the course of 10 years. Heywood Road in Prestwich, Bury, has been closed, and traffic diverted, after two or three large cracks caused the tarmac to dip dramatically. It is the third sinkhole on the road within a decade, with one first appearing in 2016 and another occurring on the same street in 2023. The area has been cordoned off while the utility company assesses the site "to determine the cause". Image caption, A sinkhole has twice previously appeared on Heywood Road prior to the collapse this month - once in 2016 and again in 2023 The previous sinkholes, in 2016 and 2023, followed sewer collapses. A United Utilities spokesperson said: "We have engineers on site carrying out further assessments to determine the cause of the sinkhole and establish whether it is linked to any United Utilities assets." input.summary: The Wigan hospital had one of the country's worst record for A&E waits
input.evidence_text: Royal Albert Edward Infirmary failings revealed in damning report - BBC News Image source, Google Image caption, The Royal Albert Edward Infirmary's urgent and emergency care and medical care had been previously rated as "good" by inspectors By Lynette Horsburgh North West Published 16 September 2026 Records show a hospital trust is "among the worst in England" for people spending more than 12 hours in the emergency department. More than 900 people faced stays of such length in the month prior to a damning inspection. The Care Quality Commission (CQC) has downgraded urgent and emergency care at Royal Albert Edward Infirmary in Wigan, Greater Manchester, after several concerns were raised over patient care. A warning notice has been issued over the triage system, the identification of sepsis and how those with mental health needs are cared for after the unannounced inspection in May, with "rapid improvements" called for. The trust said it was "working hard" to make improvements. The NHS watchdog previously rated the urgent and emergency care and the medical care at the hospital - which was also inspected - as "good" but has downgraded them both to "requires improvement". Inspectors said the service was not meeting any of its sepsis targets citing two cases where staff had identified potential sepsis and follow up actions had not been completed more than 18 hours later. National guidelines state they should be done within an hour. Inspectors found leaders had not ensured there were dedicated spaces to safely accommodate high-risk young people with mental health needs, with some staff saying they had experienced physical and psychological harm as a result. input.summary: Judges reject the Attorney General's bid to increase Morsal Mohammed Naim's sentence
input.evidence_text: Morsal Mohammed Naim: Jail term for toddler's death not increased - BBC News Image source, GMP Image caption, Omra Wali Jan was two when she died in February 2024. By Haider Saleem Reporting from North West Published 16 September 2026 A mother who shook her two-year-old daughter to death will not have her nine-year sentence increased after Court of Appeal judges ruled it was not "unduly lenient". Morsal Mohammed Naim, 33, of Levenshulme, admitted manslaughter and child cruelty after her daughter, Omra Wali Jan, suffered a catastrophic brain injury and later died. The Attorney General referred the sentence imposed at Manchester Crown Court in February. However, three senior judges rejected the challenge, despite saying they would have imposed a longer term. Lord Justice Bean said the original sentence fell within the range available to the trial judge and described the circumstances of the case as "exceptional and extreme". Warning: This article contains distressing details Image source, GMP Image caption, Morsal Mohammed Naim was jailed for nine years after admitting manslaughter and child cruelty Omra, who was aged two years and three months, had suffered repeated abuse before her death, including burns caused by the metal of a cigarette lighter. Police were called to reports of an unresponsive child in Levenshulme on 30 November 2023. Naim initially told paramedics her daughter had choked on a biscuit. Before pleading guilty, she claimed Omra had choked, fallen and hit her head on a baby bouncer and that she had shaken her in an attempt to revive her. Doctors later found Omra had suffered a brain injury as well as other unexplained injuries, including burns, bruising and a fractured rib. title: RSPCA animal welfare and rehabilitation campus moves step closer

input.lead: The RSPCA plans to build the "one stop shop" for animals in need in Pennington Flash in Leigh, Wigan
input.summary: The RSPCA plans to build the "one stop shop" for animals in need in Pennington Flash in Leigh, Wigan
input.evidence_text: RSPCA animal welfare and rehabilitation campus moves step closer - BBC News Image source, RSPCA Image caption, Under the plans, the campus would have a small animal block, a ferret block and a cattery By Chris Gee Local Democracy Reporting Service Published 16 September 2026 The RSPCA's plans to build a regional animal welfare and rehabilitation campus have come a step closer. The animal welfare charity is proposing to create what it describes as a "one-stop shop" from rescue to recovery for animals most in need on farmland close to Pennington Flash in Leigh, Wigan. The charity said up to 150 jobs would be based at the Mossley Hall site if approved. It has submitted a environmental impact assessment report, published on Wigan Council's planning portal, which has been commissioned ahead of a full planning application. The document states that an "integrated animal welfare, veterinary, rehabilitation and education campus" is proposed on land at Mossley Hall on Slag Lane, Lowton, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said. Part of the site is just 50 metres (164 ft) away from the Pennington Flash nature reserve. The 15 hectare site is made up of agricultural land, a disused railway embankment and woodland. The document said the development would include clinical veterinary and behavioural facilities, rehabilitation, training and rehoming provision and administration buildings. The report said: "The main building with veterinary services and staff offices, a ferret block and an electrical substation will be located in the central south of the site. "The campus will include a small animals block, a hay barn, cattery blocks and a foul drainage treatment plant." It means St John Street is - by some distance - the worst street in Manchester for parking fines Thousands have been caught out with many criticising Manchester Council, which makes around £7m a year from parking fines across the borough. Town hall bosses have defended the number of fines on St John Street, insisting there is plentiful and clear signage alerting motorists to Some motorists claim the new arrangement is confusing as pay machines on the street mention no ban. He was serving a controversial indeterminate public protection sentence , having been jailed aged 17 for two-and-a-half years for attempted robbery The 32-year-old was released in 2022, having spent 13 years in prison, but was recalled the following year after failing a drugs test. On June 18 last year he was found hanged in his cell and died in Royal Oldham Hospital three days later Now Manchester North senior coroner Joanne Kearsley has raised urgent concerns about his death. In a prevention of future deaths report sent to the prison and the chief coroner Ms Kearsley wrote: "Upon finding Mr Hamer the prison officers did not cut the ligature for nearly three "It was heard that they panicked and were visibly distressed on finding Mr Hamer. They had undertaken their basic life support training years ago on their initial prison officer training."

Those who pay within 10 days will be eligible for a reduced payment of £700, with the full amount payable within 14 days. The landmark decision is subject to a The move is part of a wider commitment to tackle environmental crime and support the ambitions set out in Manchester's new Fly-tipping and Litter Strategy, which aims to reduce fly-tipping incidents by a third by 2035 Residents have repeatedly said cleaner streets, well-kept parks and action on environmental crime as among their top priorities for the city. Fly-tipping continues to place a significant burden on council resources, drain public money away from essential services and impact the h In 2025-26, Manchester recorded 17,954 fly-tipping incidents, resulting in the removal of more than 5,594 tonnes of waste from across the city. A total of 992 fines were issued for waste deposits in the same period The strategy supports the aims of the council's Our Manchester Strategy , which sets out a vision for cleaner, greener and better maintained neighbourhoods

Waste linked to her address was found dumped on land to the rear of Nantwich Walk in March 2026. The waste consisted of a large quantity of household rubbish, including plastic storage boxes, a glass table, toys, a travel cot, refuse bags and shopping bags. During investigation, Ms Connell confirmed she had arranged for a third party to remove household waste from her property but was unable to demonstrate that it had been disposed of lawfully by a licenced carrier. The court handed her a one day custodial sentence and ordered her to pay costs of £432 and a victim surcharge of £26. Cllr Robert Morrisey, Bolton Council’s Executive Cabinet Member for Regulatory Services, said: “The case serves as a stark reminder that those who don’t dispose of their waste lawfully face significant consequences, including court action, fines, costs and, in some circumstances, imprisonment. "Fly-tipping blights neighbourhoods, damages the environment and places an unnecessary burden on taxpayers who ultimately have to fund the clean-up.
